Jallianwala Bagh. The massacre took place on April 13, 1919, in Amritsar, Punjab, when British Brigadier General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire without warning into a peaceful gathering of Indian civilians in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh. Between 379 and 1,200 people were killed, and over 1,000 more were wounded. The massacre occurred amid widespread protests against the Rowlatt Acts, repressive wartime legislation that authorized detention without trial, and marked a decisive rupture between British colonial rule and the Indian independence movement. The slaughter of unarmed civilians, including women and children, crystallized Indian nationalist sentiment and made armed revolution seem inevitable.

The British had enacted the Rowlatt Acts in March 1919, extending wartime emergency powers and allowing indefinite detention without trial. Indian nationalist leaders and the press denounced the laws as draconian, and widespread satyagraha—nonviolent civil disobedience—protests erupted across Punjab. Agitation in Amritsar intensified, and British authorities banned public gatherings and arrested prominent nationalist leaders.

On April 13, Baisakhi, the Sikh and Hindu spring harvest festival, thousands of Indians—men, women, and children—gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden with few exits. The meeting was ostensibly to discuss the arrests and the Rowlatt Acts. Speakers included nationalist figures and religious leaders. Most attendees were unaware that Dyer had issued a ban on all public assemblies, and the gathering was not explicitly defiant but rather coincided with the festival.

Brigadier General Reginald Dyer arrived with approximately 90 Gurkha and Sikh soldiers. Upon seeing the crowd, he immediately ordered them to fire without warning or demand for dispersal. Soldiers fired 1,650 rounds into the densely packed, panicked crowd for 10 minutes, and people were crushed in the stampede toward the single exit. Dyer left without tending the wounded, and bodies lay in the garden overnight. Official British estimates placed deaths at 379, but Indian sources and modern historians claim closer to 1,000.

Martial law was imposed across Punjab, and further protests were violently suppressed. Dyer was initially hailed by the British community in India and became a symbol of colonial intransigence. The Indian press and nationalists erupted with outrage, and the massacre unified previously divided factions of the independence movement.

An official inquiry, the Hunter Commission of 1920, concluded Dyer had acted unjustifiably but without malice. He was relieved of command but not court-martialed. Later, Dyer was denounced by Britain itself as having acted without authority. He became a pariah in official circles but remained celebrated by right-wing British imperialists. The massacre vindicated Mohandas Gandhi's earlier warnings that British rule rested on force, not consent, and accelerated support for his Non-Cooperation Movement and later independence struggle. Jallianwala Bagh stands as a watershed moment in the history of decolonization, demonstrating that the British Raj, despite its claim to civilized governance, would resort to mass killing of unarmed civilians to suppress dissent. It destroyed the fiction of a benevolent British civilizing mission and united Indian nationalists in the conviction that independence was not negotiable but inevitable.
